subjects.displayTitle: The power and sovereignty of God: He doeth whatsoever He willeth
subjects.introduction: To call God all-powerful is easy; to live inside that knowledge is the work of a lifetime. Bahá’u’lláh bears witness to a sovereignty that had no beginning and will have no end, a dominion that would not shrink by a single atom if every kingdom of earth and heaven were given away, and a will without whose leave not a leaf stirs. That He does whatever He wills runs through the prayers like a pulse, and it raises hard questions. If every created power is weak before Him, why is injustice given respite, and what is left for human effort, medicine and planning? The answers lie in a patience that outruns the might behind it, in decrees that work through means and causes, and in a power that chose to appear in the garment of a prisoner and to seek no kingdom but the hearts of men. From here the path leads on to the freedom of the divine will, to the justice that tempers it, and to the names of God by which so many prayers end.

order.why: These readings begin with a sovereignty that has no beginning and no end. Bahá’u’lláh bears witness that God’s sovereignty can never perish nor His will be altered, that from everlasting He has been King of the entire creation and its Prime Mover, and that were He to bestow the kingdoms of earth and heaven on one creature, His dominion would not diminish by even an atom. The Báb writes that from everlasting God has been alone, with no created thing approaching His station, that His sovereignty in His realm had no beginning and shall have no end, and that the Messengers were sent to manifest His power over creation, not for His own sake. In reported talks ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reasons that the sovereignty of God is not accidental but eternal, that a king without a kingdom is impossible, and that creatures have therefore always existed, while the worlds of God are numberless. Read together, these passages ask what it means for a power to be complete in itself and still to be exercised.

These readings look for God’s power in the created world and in the Word that brings it into being. The Báb speaks of God calling all things into being by His injunction “Be”, and of God being at every moment engaged in a wondrous work and a new creation. Bahá’u’lláh marvels at the power that makes spring and autumn appear at a single time and produces light from fire and joy from sorrow, says that all the atoms of the earth bear witness to that power, and challenges those who claim lordship to produce a single bubble upon the water. In reported talks ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes that no one could create a single grain, that all created things are captive to the law of nature except the divine power, and that God brings fire from stone and flowers from black dust. The section ends with the Word itself: the heavens may vanish, but what the Pen has revealed shall never pass away, and one verse outweighs the treasuries of all creation.
shortened: Sanctified be the Lord of all mankind, at the mention of Whose name all the atoms of the earth have been made to vibrate, and the Tongue of Grandeur hath been moved to disclose that which had been wrapt in His knowledge and lay concealed within the treasury of His might. He, verily, through the potency of His name, the Mighty, the All-Powerful, the Most High, is the ruler of all that is in the heavens and all that is on earth.

In reported talks ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes that no one could create a single grain, that all created things are captive to the law of nature except the divine power, and that God brings fire from stone and flowers from black dust. The section ends with the Word itself: the heavens may vanish, but what the Pen has revealed shall never pass away, and one verse outweighs the treasuries of all creation.
shortened: Glorified, immeasurably glorified art Thou, in Whose hands is the empire of whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on earth, Thou, Who through but one word of Thy mouth, caused all things to expire and dissolve asunder, and Who, by yet another word, caused whatever had been separated to be combined and reunited! Magnified be Thy name, O Thou Who hast power over all that are in the heavens and all that are on earth, Whose dominion embraceth whatsoever is in the heaven of Thy Revelation and the kingdom of Thy creation.

These readings dwell on the phrase that recurs throughout the subject: He doeth whatsoever He willeth. Bahá’u’lláh writes that God bestows His favor on whom He wills and takes it from whom He wills, that the Will of God has triumphed over the will of His creatures, and that not a leaf stirs save by His leave. He adds that God has not desired that every soul should do whatever it wills, and that all He ordains is for the good of His servants. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that the servant can do nothing of his own will alone, that the pen of destiny is in the hand of divine decree and not of human design, and that if creation went forward by only one rule the all-encompassing Power could not make itself felt. Other passages qualify how this is understood: Bahá’u’lláh says that every matter has its appointed time and that divine decrees work through means and causes, and a reported talk compares God to the Captain of a ship whose mate is the Covenant.

He adds that God has not desired that every soul should do whatever it wills, and that all He ordains is for the good of His servants. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that the servant can do nothing of his own will alone, that the pen of destiny is in the hand of divine decree and not of human design, and that if creation went forward by only one rule the all-encompassing Power could not make itself felt. Other passages qualify how this is understood: Bahá’u’lláh says that every matter has its appointed time and that divine decrees work through means and causes, and a reported talk compares God to the Captain of a ship whose mate is the Covenant.
shortened: Praise be unto Him Who hath revealed laws in accordance with His good-pleasure. Verily, He is sovereign over whatsoever He wisheth.

These readings set the power of God beside the weakness of everything else. In prayer after prayer Bahá’u’lláh confesses that every possessor of greatness is as nothing before God’s greatness, that the mighty have acknowledged their weakness and the learned their ignorance, that every conqueror is but a serf whom His hand has subjected, and that even the holy Ones and the Prophets confess their helplessness before the revelations of His might. His prayers have the believer testify to his own powerlessness and poverty before God’s might and wealth, and the Báb writes, Say, God is the Lord and all are worshippers unto Him. The same power also lifts up. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that when the Omnipotent Lord glances upon a powerless servant, that servant becomes a mine of might; a reported talk says the aid of the Most High turns a drop into an ocean and a gnat into an eagle; and Bahá’u’lláh says His might can raise a straw to the galaxies while returning the possessors of palaces to their graves.
shortened: I testify, at this moment, to my powerlessness and to Thy might, to my poverty and to Thy wealth. There is none other God but Thee, the Help in Peril, the Self-Subsisting.

In prayer after prayer Bahá’u’lláh confesses that every possessor of greatness is as nothing before God’s greatness, that the mighty have acknowledged their weakness and the learned their ignorance, that every conqueror is but a serf whom His hand has subjected, and that even the holy Ones and the Prophets confess their helplessness before the revelations of His might. His prayers have the believer testify to his own powerlessness and poverty before God’s might and wealth, and the Báb writes, Say, God is the Lord and all are worshippers unto Him. These readings ask why a God of such power allows what He allows. Bahá’u’lláh calls God the One Whose strength is immense and Whose decree is terrible, Who deals equitably with all in heaven and on earth and causes men to die through His wrath, and the Báb speaks of the Day of Severing when He shall judge through the power of Truth. Yet most of the section concerns His forbearance. A prayer of Bahá’u’lláh marvels at God’s patience despite His power and His forbearance despite His might; another says that His forbearance with the idolaters is due to a wisdom concealed from His servants; and Bahá’u’lláh says that had not His mercy preceded all things, He would have returned existence to nothingness. The Báb writes that delay in a decree for the loved ones is no sign of impotence, nor is respite for the enemy a sign of restraint. In a reported talk ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that God is not impotent and could remove every barrier, but that great wisdom is concealed in sufferings which only the pure-hearted discern.
shortened: He is supreme over His servants, and standeth over His creatures. In His hand is the source of authority and truth. He maketh men alive by His signs, and causeth them to die through His wrath. He shall not be asked of His doings, and His might is equal unto all things. He is the Potent, the All-Subduing. He holdeth within His grasp the empire of all things, and on His right hand is fixed the Kingdom of His Revelation. His power, verily, embraceth the whole of creation.

These readings turn from God’s power over creation to the power revealed through His Manifestation. In the Súriy-i-Haykal God addresses the Living Temple, placing in His right hand the empire of all things and ordaining Him the source of all existence in the new creation, that all may know His power to accomplish what He has purposed through His word “Be”. Bahá’u’lláh writes that His proof is the greatness of His might and sovereignty, that His signs have encompassed the earth, and that the Most Mighty Bell has appeared in the form of Him Who is the Most Great Name. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes how within a short span Bahá’u’lláh stirred up the East and the West, and cites the words that the Dawning-place of God’s Cause has no partner in the Most Great Infallibility and is the Manifestation of “He doeth whatsoever He willeth”. Other passages say that God, not men, selects the Promised One, and that were He to pronounce black to be white, none may ask wherefore or why.
shortened: We, verily, have ordained this Temple to be the source of all existence in the new creation, that all may know of a certainty My power to accomplish that which I have purposed through My word "Be", and it is!

O Living Temple!  Stretch forth Thy hand over all who are in heaven and on earth, and seize within the grasp of Thy Will the reins of command.  We have, verily, placed in Thy right hand the empire of all things.  Do as Thou willest, and fear not the ignorant.

Other passages say that God, not men, selects the Promised One, and that were He to pronounce black to be white, none may ask wherefore or why.
shortened: Thou art He, by Whose name the Hidden Secret was divulged, and the Well-Guarded Name was revealed, and the seals of the sealed-up Goblet were opened, shedding thereby its fragrance over all creation, whether of the past or of the future.

order.why: These readings concern a power that appeared in what looked like its opposite. Bahá’u’lláh writes that if absolute power appears in the garment of powerlessness, and the Absolute Sovereign appears as one ruled and oppressed, there is wisdom in it; that a glory no abasement can approach has shone forth from the horizon of the prison; and that without armies, means or weapons He summoned all to God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that though imprisoned He was the Ruler of what was and what would be, and that though alone and forsaken He subdued the realm of being. Recorded and reported accounts add particulars. Bahá’u’lláh’s own words recall that He stayed in Tihran amid danger because God willed to manifest His Cause. These readings set earthly rule beside the sovereignty of God. In the Lawh-i-Ra’ís Bahá’u’lláh warns those who wronged Him that, should it be His wish, God would scatter them in dust; in a prayer He confesses that all kings are but God’s servants; and in the Epistle to the Son of the Wolf He prays that God may assist the kings of the earth. The Báb warns a king that all dominion is in God’s hand like a ring upon a finger, which He turns as He wills, and in the Qayyúmu’l-Asmá’ says, Let not sovereignty deceive thee, for every soul shall taste of death. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that the Apostles of Christ, once fishermen, now hold the real sovereignty, while the sovereignty of kings is temporal. In reported talks He calls God the real king and the others figureheads, says a material ruler is mighty by the sword or by votes while the Heavenly Ruler is mighty through divine bounty, and tells how Tamerlane consoled Bayezid by saying that God does not value worldly sovereignty as much as a mosquito’s wing.
shortened: Whosoever Thou exaltest is raised above the angels, and attaineth the station: 'Verily, We uplifted him to a place on  high!'; and whosoever Thou dost abase is made lower than dust, nay, less than nothing. O Divine Providence! Though wicked, sinful, and intemperate, we still seek from Thee a 'seat of truth,' and long to behold the countenance of the Omnipotent King. It is Thine to command, and all sovereignty belongeth to Thee, and the realm of might boweth before Thy behest.

We pray God -- exalted be His glory -- and cherish the hope that He may graciously assist the manifestations of affluence and power and the daysprings of sovereignty and glory, the kings of the earth -- may God aid them through His strengthening grace -- to establish the Lesser Peace.

His mercy hath ever preceded all else, and His grace hath outstripped all things.

order.why: These readings describe the kind of dominion God seeks. In the Kitáb-i-Aqdas Bahá’u’lláh tells the kings that it is not His wish to lay hands on their kingdoms, for His mission is to seize and possess the hearts of men, and He bids all observe His commandments for the love of His beauty. Elsewhere He writes that He could have conquered the whole world with a single word, but gave sovereignty to sovereigns and reserved for Himself the love of the hearts of His servants, and that through the Most Exalted Word He took possession of the cities of hearts, burning away their veils. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that a true prince is the soul who conquers the realm of hearts and establishes an eternal, spiritual sovereignty. In reported talks He says that love is the eternal sovereignty and the divine power by which the kings of earth are overcome, that only the divine potency can unite hearts, and that it was the power of God that gathered His hearers in spite of cold and windy weather.

These readings bring the power of God to the needs of daily life. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that the omnipotence of God shall solve every difficulty, and that while everyone should seek medical treatment and follow the doctor’s instructions, in reality it is God Who gives healing. In reported talks He says that there is but one power which heals, and that medicine is the outward and visible means through which heavenly healing is obtained. Bahá’u’lláh prays that water and sun, God’s two great signs, may not be withheld, since they are effective only by His leave, and promises that whoever makes His love a breastplate and His Cause a fortress will be harmed by no venom, fire or water. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that humans and jinn together could not pluck a single hair from the head of one of the friends. In a reported talk He says that if God wills to protect a man a little ship may escape destruction, where the greatest vessel with the most skillful navigator may not survive.
shortened: God be thanked, that promised aid hath been vouchsafed, as is plain for all to see, and it shineth forth as clear as the sun in the heavens.

Water and sun are Thy two great signs - deprive not Thy servants of these two. By Thy leave they are effective, and without it they neither nourish nor satisfy, and thus shall it ever be. order.why: These readings are longer prayers that turn the knowledge of God’s power into petition. Bahá’u’lláh’s prayers ask God, by His power that has encompassed all created things and His sovereignty that has transcended the entire creation, to lift the one who prays up to the heaven of His holiness, to subdue His servants by the Name He has made King of all names, and to draw them through His utterances to the Dawning-Place of His inspiration. One prayer has the limbs of the body testify to His unity and the hair of the head to the power of His sovereignty; another turns to Him by His sovereignty, forsaking the will and desire of the one who prays. Others confess that none can help God but His own Self, or ask that the ensigns of His triumph be lifted up. The Báb writes that whenever He attempts to approach God He perceives nothing in Himself but the tokens of God’s grace, and prays by the splendour before which fire is turned into light.

order.why: The guide closes with the confession that ends prayer after prayer. Gathered together, these short sentences show how the subject of this guide lives inside devotion. After asking for something, the one who prays acknowledges that God is able to grant it and calls on Him by one of His names. Read slowly, the repetition becomes a study of the names themselves, and of what each one says about the power to which the prayer is addressed.

In these authorized words from a prayer of Bahá’u’lláh, the prayer tells God that He beholds His servants in the abyss of perdition and error, and asks where is His light of divine guidance and, since He knows their helplessness and feebleness, where is His power, O Thou in Whose grasp lie the powers of heaven and earth. Placed after the prayers of the guide, it turns the subject into a plea on behalf of others: the power of God is invoked for those who have lost their way.

In these authorized words from a prayer of Bahá’u’lláh, the one who prays implores the Lord of all being, Who overshadows all things visible and invisible, by His Name whereby He has subdued the hearts and the souls of men, and by the billows of the Ocean of His mercy and the splendors of the Daystar of His bounty. questions: The readings say that God’s sovereignty has no beginning and that a king without a kingdom is impossible, yet also that God is independent of all things. How do the sections on eternal sovereignty and on creation help you hold these together?

Many passages repeat that He doeth whatsoever He willeth, while others say that every matter has its appointed time and that divine decrees work through means and causes. What does the section on the divine will suggest about the place of human effort, medicine and planning?

Bahá’u’lláh marvels at God’s patience despite His power, and the Báb says that respite for the enemy is no sign of restraint. How do the readings on forbearance respond to the question of why suffering and injustice are allowed to continue?

Bahá’u’lláh writes that absolute power may appear in the garment of powerlessness. Using the accounts of His imprisonment and of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s release, consider what kind of power the section on sovereignty in prison describes.

In the Kitáb-i-Aqdas Bahá’u’lláh says that His mission is to seize and possess the hearts of men, not to lay hands on kingdoms. How do the sections on kings and on hearts change the meaning of the words power and sovereignty?
About a sixth of the guide is the short refrain Potent art Thou to do what Thou willest. Choose one closing name of God from that section and consider how it shapes the prayer it ends.
